summary: Tarpaulin Cove light on Naushon Island, first shown by a tavern keeper in 1759. The tower date is disputed (1856 or 1891); automated 1941; offered for transfer in 2024.

lens.where: A fifth-order Fresnel lens was bought in 1856 (LighthouseFriends); a fourth-order cut-glass Fresnel-type lens was installed in 1967 (nomination). The sources read do not say where either lens went.

structures.note: Brick tower. The Board's FY1891 report gives a 28-foot tower built in 1891 on the 1817 foundation; the nomination and the 2024 GSA notice give 1856 and 38 feet. Disputed; see notes.

access.note: Naushon Island is private and the public is not allowed to land. The tower is not open to the public.

facts.agency: Cuttyhunk Historical Society (license from the Coast Guard, 2001); excess to Coast Guard needs as of July 2024; GSA offering it for transfer

events.note: A private light kept by tavern keepers at the cove, begun by Zaccheus Lumbert in 1759 (LighthouseFriends; Cuttyhunk Historical Society). Not a federal light.
Land ceded by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts (nomination).
Federal site bought for $216; rubblestone tower begun, costing $6,062.11 (LighthouseFriends). The nomination says the light was first manned in 1817.
Fixed white light first shown October 1817 with John Hayden as keeper (LighthouseFriends).
Fifth-order Fresnel lens from Sautter and Company, Paris, installed in place of nine lamps (LighthouseFriends).
The nomination and the 2024 GSA notice date the white brick tower to 1856. The Board's FY1891 report describes a different sequence; disputed.
Changed from fixed white to fixed white punctuated every thirty seconds by a flash, 7 April 1870 (LighthouseFriends).

Old 1817 rubble tower demolished; brick tower 28 feet high built on the same foundation with iron stairs, iron deck and fourth-order lantern (Board FY1891). Light shown from a temporary structure 25 April to 30 June 1891.
Boathouse moved to a better site on the west side of the cove, refloored, underpinned and protected by a retaining wall (Board FY1899).
Oil house added to the station (LighthouseFriends).
Changed from oil to incandescent oil vapor (Bulletin 1914).
Keeper Frank A. Davis helped two men from a schooner that caught fire and burned near the light, 31 October 1924; a doctor was fetched from Woods Hole. LighthouseFriends says both men died.
The great New England hurricane of 21 September 1938 destroyed the fog-bell tower, which was not rebuilt (LighthouseFriends; nomination).
Light automated; mariners told of the change for about 30 September 1941 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS; Cuttyhunk Historical Society).
Candlepower reduced to 700 (nomination: from 4,500; LighthouseFriends: from 7,500).
Keepers' dwelling and other buildings demolished (nomination; LighthouseFriends).
Coast Guard issued the Cuttyhunk Historical Society a 25-year license to care for the site and structure.
Coast Guard declared the light excess to its needs (July 2024); GSA notice of availability at no cost to eligible entities, with 60 days for letters of interest.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Board's FY1891 report gives a rebuilt tower of 28 feet on the 1817 foundation; the nomination's chronology gives 1856 and 38 feet and its description 78 feet; the 2024 GSA notice gives 1856 and 38 feet; the Cuttyhunk Historical Society gives 1891. LighthouseFriends quotes Board records listing the 1817 tower at 25 feet. The story reports the disagreement and follows the Board's 1891 account.

notes_for_editor: FACT-CHECK 2026-10-22 (independent check; story and this record revised). UNRESOLVED CONFLICTS: (1) The brick tower's date and height: the Board's FY1891 entry (129, scan p.62) gives a brick tower 28 feet high built on the 1817 foundation in 1891; the nomination's chronology gives 1856 and 38 feet, its description 78 feet ('78' cylindrical white brick tower (1856)'), and it notes a 1891 remodel; the 2024 GSA notice gives 1856 and 38 feet; the Cuttyhunk Historical Society gives 1891; LighthouseFriends gives 28 feet for the present tower, and says some reports give the 1817 tower 38 feet while Board records list it at 25 feet. The story gives the Board's 1891 account and states the 1856 dates. (2) Candlepower in 1958: nomination 4,500 to 700; LighthouseFriends 7,500 to 700. (3) Keeper Spencer's start: roster 1925; LighthouseFriends 'since 1928'. (4) Keeper's name: roster 'Carl D. Hill' (1916-1920); Commissioner of Lighthouses 1920 'Carl P. Hill, keeper' (scan p.554). (5) The 1924 schooner's name is garbled in the Bulletin OCR ('TaMlI Bitter8'); LighthouseFriends gives 'Tanzy Bitters'. The story does not name the schooner. The Bulletin's 'explosion' is in garbled OCR ('e:q>losion') but the word is clear enough to keep; LighthouseFriends also says explosion. (6) Keepers' dwelling: nomination gives 1890 at $3,000; LighthouseFriends gives 1888 at $3,000. Not stated in the story. (7) Status after July 2024: the GSA notice opened a 60-day window; no transfer decision is recorded in the sources read. Verify before publication. (8) Naushon: GSA calls it a private island; LighthouseFriends says the Forbes family holds it on a second 99-year lease from the government. The story says only that it is private. (9) The 1759 date rests on LighthouseFriends and the Cuttyhunk Historical Society's own statement; no primary record of a 1759 light was read. (10) The 1920 Commissioner entry is quoted for the name only. (11) ROSTER: matched by name and position (0.09 km). Two contractors on the roster (Benjamin Beall, Duncan M.B. Thaxter) have no dates and are kept as 'other' lines. (12) SEARCH: Chronicling America 'Tarpaulin Cove' hits in Massachusetts papers (1891 Springfield Republican, page 12) concern a vessel that mistook another cove for Tarpaulin; not the light, not used. (13) LF-ONLY FACTS, no primary record read: Lumbert's 1759 light and 1762 letter, the 1764 sale, the Hayden log, the 1842 inspection statement (quoted by LighthouseFriends), Norton and the Alabama, the Olive Davis detail, the 1870 characteristic change, the 1903 oil house, the 1958 and 1962 details, the open house and closure, and the Forbes lease. (14) Olive Davis is recorded as an acting keeper here (LighthouseFriends); she is not a keeper of record on the USLHS roster. The story names her only as Frank Davis's wife. (15) The 1864 Board rules are general period context, marked in the story; the rule reads 'failing to give timely notice of the want of oil, wicks, or chimneys'. (16) OCR TABLE CHECKS: the FY1891 Board entry 129 (scan p.62) is read from its printed line text ('The old tower of rubble mason ly, built in 1817, was demolished'), not by column position. The FY1891 entry gives a 1,200-pound bell struck by machinery, not a fog bell; the story says bell.
